    AI Overview
    The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) of 1978 is a U.S. federal law regulating the surveillance of foreign powers and agents within the United States. It requires intelligence agencies to obtain warrants from a specialized court—the FISA Court (FISC)—to conduct wiretapping, physical searches, and acquire business records, primarily targeting non-U.S. persons. 
    Key aspects of FISA include: 
    • Purpose: Enacted to prevent privacy abuses by the government, FISA authorizes surveillance to collect foreign intelligence information.
    • FISA Court (FISC): A special court, composed of federal judges, that reviews government applications for electronic surveillance and search warrants in nonpublic sessions.
    • Section 702 (Controversial): Part of the law that allows for surveillance of non-Americans located outside the U.S., which often sweeps up the communications of Americans they are in contact with, allowing the NSA and FBI to access this data without a warrant, say critics at the Brennan Center for Justice and ACLU.
    • Reauthorization: Congress regularly updates the law, with recent debates focusing on strengthening privacy protections for Americans versus maintaining the ability to track foreign threats.

    People also ask
    Does FISA apply to U.S. citizens?
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    Yes, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) applies to U.S. citizens. While primarily designed for foreign intelligence, FISA regulates surveillance of "U.S. persons"—including citizens and permanent residents—when they are targeted or when their communications are incidentally collected, particularly under FISA Section 702. 
    Key Aspects of FISA and U.S. Citizens: 
    • Targeted Surveillance: To target a U.S. citizen inside the U.S. for electronic surveillance, the government must show probable cause to the [Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court (FISC)] that the target is a foreign power or an agent of a foreign power.
    • Section 702 and Incidental Collection:
      Section 702 targets non-U.S. persons located outside the U.S., but it often collects communications from Americans communicating with those foreign targets.
    • "Minimization" Requirements: FISA mandates "minimization procedures" to limit the retention and dissemination of U.S. person information collected in these investigations.
    • FBI Queries: The FBI can search, or "query," this database of collected information for U.S. person information, a practice that has raised significant privacy concerns. 
    Under certain FISA authorities, particularly in domestic cases, the government must meet heightened requirements, ensuring that surveillance is focused on intelligence rather than domestic criminal investigation.
